chapters.n: Nahum’s message is a “burden” — a heavy oracle — against Nineveh, capital of Assyria. About a century after Jonah, Nineveh had returned to cruelty. Nahum likely spoke between 663 and 612 BC, when Nineveh fell.

f.g: A weighty prophetic message, usually of judgment.
His name means “comfort” — his message comforted Judah, oppressed by Assyria.
From Elkosh, a village whose location is uncertain.

chapters.n: God is fiercely protective of His people and will repay His enemies. His “vengeance” is not petty revenge but justice against oppressors who refuse to repent.

f.g: Zealous, passionately devoted to His covenant people.

chapters.n: God is patient, but He won’t let the guilty go unpunished forever. His power shows in storms; the clouds are just dust kicked up by His feet.

f.w: The LORD is slow to anger
the clouds are the dust of his feet
f.g: A striking image of God’s greatness: storm clouds are like dust from His steps.

chapters.n: He commands the sea and dries up rivers, as at the Red Sea and Jordan. Even the most fertile places — Bashan, Carmel, Lebanon — wither before Him.

f.g: Rich pasture land east of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: Mountains shake and hills melt in His presence; the whole earth trembles.
Who can withstand His anger? His fury pours out like fire and shatters rocks.
Yet in the middle of the storm: “The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble.” He knows and cares for those who trust Him. The same power that judges protects.

f.w: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble
he knoweth them that trust in him

chapters.n: With an overwhelming flood He will end Nineveh. Ancient sources report that flooding helped breach Nineveh’s defenses in 612 BC.
Whatever Assyria plots against the Lord will fail. He will finish it so completely that trouble won’t need to come twice.

f.w: What do ye imagine against the LORD?

chapters.n: Like tangled thorns and staggering drunks, the enemies will be burned up like dry straw.

f.g: Entangled like thornbushes — which burn quickly.

chapters.n: A wicked counselor came from Nineveh who plotted against the Lord — perhaps King Sennacherib, who besieged Jerusalem.
Though Assyria is strong and numerous, it will be cut down. To Judah, God says: “I afflicted you, but I won’t afflict you anymore.”

f.w: I will afflict thee no more

chapters.n: God will break Assyria’s yoke off Judah’s neck and snap the chains of their oppression.

f.w: I break his yoke from off thee

chapters.n: To Assyria’s king God decrees: your dynasty will end, your idols will be destroyed, and I will prepare your grave.

f.w: no more of thy name be sown
f.g: You will have no descendants to carry on your name.
An idol cast from metal.

chapters.n: Look! A messenger runs across the mountains with good news of peace. Judah can again celebrate its feasts, for the oppressor is gone. Isaiah used the same words, and Abinadi applied them to those who publish the gospel.

f.w: the feet of him that bringeth good tidings

chapters.n: Nahum sarcastically warns Nineveh to prepare: the attacker is coming — guard the walls, watch the roads, brace yourselves! It won’t help. Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC.

f.g: The “scatterer” or “shatterer” — the invading army.
Fortress or ramparts.

chapters.n: The Lord is restoring Jacob’s glory, which plunderers like Assyria had stripped like a ravaged vine.

f.g: Better, “restored” or “brought back.”
Plunderers — Assyria had emptied Israel.

chapters.n: The attackers’ shields are red and soldiers dressed in scarlet; chariots flash like fire, and spears are brandished. The Medes and Babylonians were known for red shields and clothing.

f.g: Spears made of cypress wood, being brandished.

chapters.n: Chariots race madly through the streets, jostling in the squares, flashing like torches and darting like lightning.

f.g: Jostle, collide.

chapters.n: Nineveh’s king summons his best officers, but they stumble as they rush to defend the wall. The attackers set up a protective shield for the battering ram.

f.g: Nobles; elite officers.
A mantelet — a large shield protecting siege workers.

chapters.n: The river gates burst open, and the palace collapses. Nineveh sat by the Tigris and smaller rivers; flooding helped bring down its walls.

f.g: Melts away; collapses.

chapters.n: Nineveh’s queen — or the city itself, or its goddess — is stripped and carried away, while her servants moan like doves and beat their breasts.

f.g: Meaning uncertain: possibly the queen, a goddess statue, or “it is decreed.”
Beating, like a drum (tabor).

chapters.n: Nineveh had been like a full pool, but its people drain away. “Stop! Stop!” they cry, but no one turns back.

f.g: Once full and teeming with people and wealth.

chapters.n: “Take the silver! Take the gold!” Nineveh’s endless treasures, gathered by plundering other nations, are now plundered.

f.g: Precious objects and valuables.

chapters.n: The city is empty, void, and wasted. In Hebrew this sounds like a string of echoing words (buqah umebuqah umebullaqah). Hearts melt and knees knock in terror.

f.g: A rhyming Hebrew phrase meaning utter devastation.

chapters.n: Where is the lions’ den now? Assyria’s kings loved to portray themselves as lions — and they preyed on nations without fear.

f.g: Lions were a royal symbol in Assyrian art; kings boasted of lion hunts.

chapters.n: The lion killed and filled its den with prey for its cubs and mates. Assyria grew rich by tearing apart other peoples.

f.g: Prey; plunder torn away.

chapters.n: “I am against you,” says the Lord of hosts. Assyria’s chariots will burn, its young warriors fall, and its messengers — who once delivered threats like those to Hezekiah — will be silenced.
Woe to Nineveh, the city of bloodshed, full of lies and plunder, never letting go of its victims. Assyria was infamous for brutality against conquered peoples.

f.g: It never stops plundering.

chapters.n: Nahum paints a battle scene with sounds: cracking whips, rumbling wheels, galloping horses, bouncing chariots.

f.g: Prancing, galloping.

chapters.n: Flashing swords and glittering spears; bodies pile up so high that soldiers stumble over them. Assyria’s own violence returns on it.
Nineveh is pictured as a seductive prostitute and sorceress who lured and enslaved nations by charm, trade, and deception.

f.g: An attractive prostitute — a symbol of seductive power and trade.

chapters.n: “I am against you,” says the Lord. He will expose Nineveh’s shame before all nations, as a disgraced woman was publicly exposed.

f.g: Lift up your skirts — expose you.

f.w: I will shew the nations thy nakedness

chapters.n: God will throw filth on her and make her a public spectacle.

f.g: An object to be stared at in contempt.

chapters.n: Everyone who sees Nineveh will run away, saying, “It’s ruined! Who will mourn for her?” No one will comfort her.
Are you better than Thebes? That great Egyptian city on the Nile, protected by water, fell to Assyria itself in 663 BC.

f.g: No-Amon, Thebes in Upper Egypt (near modern Luxor).
The Nile, wide like a sea.

chapters.n: Thebes had powerful allies — Ethiopia, Egypt, Put, and Libya — and seemingly limitless strength.

f.g: Cush, the kingdom south of Egypt, which ruled Egypt at that time.
Peoples of North Africa; Lubim are Libyans.

chapters.n: Yet Thebes was captured: children killed, nobles divided by lottery, leaders put in chains. What Assyria did to others will be done to Assyria.

f.w: they cast lots for her honourable men

chapters.n: Nineveh too will stagger as if drunk, hide, and search for refuge from the enemy.
Its fortresses will fall as easily as ripe figs drop into a mouth when the tree is shaken.

f.g: Early figs, which fall at the slightest shake.

chapters.n: Nineveh’s soldiers will be weak and helpless, its gates wide open, its bars burned.

f.w: thy people in the midst of thee are women
f.g: An ancient insult meaning the troops will be powerless.

chapters.n: Ironic advice: stock up water for the siege, strengthen your forts, make more bricks! None of it will matter.

f.g: Mix mud and straw with the feet to make bricks.

chapters.n: Fire and sword will consume Nineveh like locusts devour a field. Even if Nineveh multiplies like locusts, it will not survive.

f.g: A kind of locust in its young stage.

chapters.n: Nineveh’s merchants were as countless as stars, but like locusts they strip the land and fly away.

f.g: Sheds its skin and flies off.

chapters.n: Assyria’s officials are like locusts huddled in a hedge on a cold day; when the sun comes out they vanish without a trace.

f.g: Guards or officials.

chapters.n: Speaking directly to Assyria’s king: your shepherds (leaders) sleep in death, your nobles lie in the dust, and your people are scattered with no one to gather them.
Your wound is fatal. Everyone who hears of your fall will clap with joy — for who has not suffered from your endless cruelty? Assyria never recovered after 612 BC.

f.g: Report, news.
